ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: wishes and promises
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How wishes work, and what granting, promising, refusing and ignoring do.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Don't promise a bed you don't have the wood for.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists make wishes that fit their situation, their traits and what the colony can actually build. Each wish has a deadline, and the council can answer it in four ways. The page "what colonists wish for" lists every kind of wish and when it comes up.

li.heading: The four answers

table.li: Answer | What happens

Grant | The colonist is pleased, trusts the council more and is always motivated (faster work for a few days), more so if the wish was promised. The happier they already are, the more likely the wish also brings an inspiration: creativity, a work or shooting frenzy, recruiting, surgery.

Promise | The deadline moves out by half the remaining time plus two days, and the colonist gains +4 trust right away. Some wishes are acted on as soon as you promise them: promising a party calls one, and promising a hunt marks the prey. A broken promise costs far more than an ordinary lapse.
Refuse | It costs a little now, and then it's settled. A refusal costs less than letting the wish lapse.

Let it lapse | The colonist takes it badly. Colonists who run out of patience sometimes do it themselves: they plan the lamp, take the bed or set their own work priorities, and trust the council less for it.

li.after: Promise only what you'll actually do in time, and refuse what you won't do.

li.heading: The rest of the colony
li.text: Other colonists react too: friends are happy for them, the jealous feel passed over, and some object openly. Watch for wishes that come with objections, since granting them pleases one colonist and annoys another.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: trust in the council
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Bitter to devoted: what trust does to mood, work and loyalty.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Answer every wish, even when the answer is no.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every colonist has a level of trust in the council: bitter, doubtful, neutral, trusting or devoted. It rises with granted wishes, kept promises and heeded petitions, falls with lapses, refusals and broken promises, and slowly drifts back toward neutral. Living under a decree they hate wears it down day by day; one they love builds it. Trust shows on the Wishes page, with its history in the tooltip.

li.heading: What it changes
li.text:
Trusting and devoted colonists work and learn faster and have fewer mental breaks; the Health tab shows this as "loyal to the council". Doubtful and bitter colonists work slower and break sooner ("grudge against the council"). Trusting colonists are also more patient with their wishes, and bitter ones less so.
Check the trust list before big decisions. It tells you who can take a disappointment and who can't.

li.heading: When someone wants to leave
li.text:
On Demanding stakes, a colonist who stays bitter for days may announce they're leaving, and walk out three days later unless their trust recovers. Children, anyone whose partner stays, and colonies of fewer than four never lose someone this way.
Granting one of their wishes or keeping a promise to them is usually enough to make them stay.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: rising standards
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Why a happy colony gets harder to please, and how to bring its standards back down.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Feed them fine meals for a season and they'll start complaining about simple ones.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
While a colonist is happy, their standards creep up from modest to comfortable, particular and spoiled. High standards make the council's rewards count for less, its letdowns hurt more, and the game's own comforts count for less. Hard times bring them back down, and so does the austerity decree.
None of this takes anything away. A colony that lives well still feels it; it just doesn't float at the top of the mood bar on a pile of small pleasures.

li.heading: How they move

table.li: Mood | Standards
Above 85% | Rise faster
About 70% to 85% | Rise
40% to about 70% | Fall slowly
Below 40% | Fall
Under austerity | Fall quickly

li.after: Ascetics barely rise; the greedy and jealous rise faster. Feasts, festivals and bonfires raise everyone's standards a little.

li.heading: Spoiled colonists
li.text: A spoiled colonist gets half the mood from the council's rewards and about 40% more from its letdowns. They're less patient, make wishes more often, reach for luxuries, and ask for more: two impressiveness levels instead of one, fine meals instead of simple ones.

li.heading: The game's comforts
li.text: Standards also reach the good moods that come from the base game and your other mods: a fine meal, an impressive bedroom, a party, a good joy activity.

table.li: Standards | Good moods from the game and other mods
Modest | In full
Comfortable | 90%
Particular | 80%
Spoiled | 70%

li.after: Only the first 10 points of each mood count for less: a +5 fine meal is +4 for a particular colonist, and a +40 catharsis is still +37 for a spoiled one. Bad moods are never touched, and Rimfolk's own good moods already follow standards, so they aren't shrunk twice. Hover a good mood in the Needs tab to see what it would be without standards. This needs the deeper game hooks; the "Standards cover the game's comforts" setting turns it off.

li.heading: When life is good
li.text:
Someone whose life is already good gets used to good things faster. When a colonist's mood is above 75%, a new good memory from Rimfolk fades sooner, smoothly down to half its usual time from 90% mood. It feels just as good while it lasts, and in hard times good things last their full length, so a lift after a bad stretch stays with them. A good memory about someone keeps its effect on opinion for the full time; only the mood ends sooner.
Everything good Rimfolk gives also shares one budget, from a wish granted to a laugh at dinner: the two biggest good moods on a colonist's mind count in full, each one after that half as much as the one before, so a dozen of them lift a colonist about as much as three. Bad moods, and the good moods of the game and other mods, aren't part of it.
The "Good times" line in a colonist's Mood tab says what these rules take off right now. Each has its own setting.

li.heading: Bringing them down
li.text: If the whole colony is particular or spoiled, a week of austerity resets expectations cheaply. You also don't have to hold every celebration: turning down a feast or a festival now and then keeps standards from climbing.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: decrees
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Policies that trade mood for output: long hours, rationing, drills and more.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Call long hours while the colony is happy, not once it's already miserable.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The Decrees page puts policies in force for a few days: up to two at once, each with a cooldown afterward. Each trades mood (and sometimes trust) for something the colony needs, or, like festival days and days of mourning, the other way around. The tab shows who will love or hate each one before you decide.

li.heading: The decrees

table.li: Decree | What it does
Long hours | Work 15% faster.
Rationing | Hunger 25% slower.
Drills | Everyone who can fight trains shooting and melee every waking hour.
Study hours | Learning 30% and research 20% faster.
Harvest push, building season, clean sweep | Faster at one kind of work.
Best behavior | Better negotiating, recruiting and trade prices.
On guard | Better aim and melee, more tiredness.
Austerity | No new wishes; standards fall fast.
Festival days | A big mood lift; work much slower; standards rise.
Days of mourning | Only while someone grieves. Grief fades much faster and mental breaks are less likely.
Quiet hours | Rest 15% faster in bed and far fewer social fights; work 5% slower.
Shared meals | Social impact up 10%, fewer social fights, some practice at talking every hour; work 3% slower.
Rest when ill | Wounds heal 20% faster and immunity builds faster; work 5% slower.
Banked fires | Fires, torches and fueled heaters burn 25% less fuel; work 4% slower.
Apprenticeships | Everyone practices construction, crafting, cooking and growing every hour; work 8% slower.
A feast day | One day: hunger 40% faster, work 15% slower, standards rise slightly.

li.after: Each decree also says something about the colony: long hours make it more hard-working, festivals more easygoing and traditional, being on guard more guarded.

li.heading: The everyday decrees
li.text:
The six newest decrees trade a few percent of work for something the colony needs, and their good moods are deliberately small. Quiet hours suit a tired or quarrelsome colony, but night owls hate them and the sociable mind losing their evenings. Shared meals help a colony full of newcomers get to know each other. Rest when ill pays off when several people are sick or hurt at once. Banked fires stretch the woodpile through a hard winter: the fuel is handed back to fires, torches and fueled heaters each hour, never to generators, to stoves while they cook, or to anything switched off. Apprenticeships spread the colony's trades so one fever can't leave it without a cook; they help the unskilled most, since practice counts for more at low levels. A feast day costs food and half a day's work for one day of good cheer.
Colonists petition for these when the moment fits: when someone is ill, in winter, or when someone new has joined.

li.heading: When to call one
li.text:
Start rationing before winter, while there's still food to save, and run drills while raids are still small. Pair a hated decree with a short one people love, or follow it with festival days.
Colonists sometimes petition for a decree when the moment fits. Declaring it within five days wins their trust.

li.heading: Repeating and forcing
li.text:
Repeating a decree within 30 days makes it harder to bear. For each recent time, those against it lose more trust in the council and resent it 35% more while it lasts. A decree still on cooldown can be forced through, at a price: it counts as one more recent time, and those against it take it badly.
Each repeat can also make someone snap: a 20% chance per recent time, 15% more when forced, at most 80%. The hot-tempered throw a tantrum; others wander off in a daze.
So space out the decrees people hate. If you must repeat one, the tab shows how many times it was used this month and the chance someone snaps. Force a decree through only in an emergency, and keep the hot-tempered busy and away from the stores while it lasts.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: dilemmas
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Hard choices where every answer costs someone something.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Whatever the council decides, someone at the table will hold it against them.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every week or so, more often while everyone is content, the council is asked to settle something: a thief, a feud, a stash, a feast, a confession, a duel, the spoils of a raid. A letter lists the answers. Colonists react according to their nature, and some answers are gambles. If you don't answer in time, the default answer is taken.

li.heading: Choosing an answer
li.text:
Some answers take real things from the stores: food, wood, silver. They're grayed out if you can't afford them.
Check the trust list first: a colonist who is already doubtful takes being overruled much harder. When kind colonists and hard ones are both present, the "fair" answer usually upsets the fewest people.

li.heading: Seasons and battles
li.text: Seasonal dilemmas (midsummer, harvest home, the longest night, naming the year) and after-battle ones (the spoils, the enemy dead, a victory feast) come up at their moment. Every dilemma and its answer is written into the chronicle and counted in the year's annals.

li.heading: Everyday life
li.text:
Many dilemmas grow out of what is happening to people right now. Someone ill when the medicine is down to a few doses; a fever that could spread through a shared room; a cook with a cold; an old family remedy, or a visitor's strange cure. A group camped on the colony's land asking for medicine, food or searchers for a lost child: how the colony answers changes how tense things are at their camp and what their people think of you. A council meeting someone missed while they were out working. A worn-out colonist (with feelings and strain on) asking for days off just when the harvest is in or the walls are broken. A squabble that grew into a feud, an elder who wants to put down the tools, a child with a question, a broken promise, the same meal or the same work every day, too many people in too little room.
Many answers call on whoever is best placed: the doctor, a forager, a tracker, a scholar, the best talker. They are grayed out when nobody fits, their skill makes a gamble less likely to go wrong, and the outcome names them. Medicine spent on someone eases their illness but never cures it outright, and no answer makes anyone sicker.
Health brings its own: a doctor who lost a patient asking for a day away, someone still convalescing who wants to be back at work (where going back too soon can make the recovery longer, never worse), family who want a say before an operation (putting it off suspends the operation until you resume it), and with Biotech, a midwife looking for an apprentice.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: names, anniversaries and annals
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How the colony remembers its people and its years.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Write the year down before people start remembering it differently.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Whoever has done the most of something earns a name for it (the Healer, Deadeye, the Kindling) until someone overtakes them. Each year since a colonist joined is marked. When a new year begins, the colony's best reader or talker writes the annals of the year that ended.

li.heading: Earning a name
li.text: Names come from the colonist's records: wounds tended, operations, kills, headshots, things built, rock mined, harvests, meals, animals tamed, prisoners recruited, research, crafting, fires fought, patients pulled through, babies delivered, and less flattering ones like messes cleaned, times on fire or mental breaks. A name moves to someone else only when they're clearly ahead, by about 15%.

li.heading: The annals
li.text: The annals cover who joined, died, left or walked out, raids, wealth, wishes, ambitions, decrees, dilemmas, friendships, feuds, trust and names. Past years can be reread from the Chronicle page.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: offices and elections
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Speaker, marshal, quartermaster, physician, steward: who holds them and what they do.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: The colony votes for the people it likes, not always the ones who are best at the job.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The council has five seats. Each gives its holder a bonus and helps the whole colony in some way. Colonists elect them once a year, voting for whoever is good at the job, has the right nature for it, and is liked. The council can appoint or dismiss anyone from the Decrees page, but overruling the vote has a cost.

table.li: Office | What it does
Speaker | Chairs every council meeting. Everyone's trust rises a little each day, at no cost to you.
Marshal | Drills train half again as fast, and the colony aims and strikes a little better.
Quartermaster | Answers to dilemmas that cost food, wood or silver cost a quarter less, and trade prices are better.
Physician | Everyone heals and fights off illness a little faster.
Steward | Standards rise a quarter more slowly, and the steward gets more out of recreation.

li.heading: Elections
li.text:
The first election comes after about a week, then one every new year. An empty seat is refilled by a by-election a few days later. No one can hold two offices, and children, slaves and lodgers can't run.
Votes follow skill, traits and friendship: friends and members of the same circle vote for each other, rivals against. Losing an election or a seat sours the loser on the winner, and can start a rivalry.
Overrule the vote only when the difference matters. The colonist who won the election will remember it.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: traditions
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What the colony keeps doing becomes expected.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Hold the midsummer feast two years running and they'll expect it every year after.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Some seasonal dilemmas have an answer the colony can make its own: a midsummer feast, a harvest celebration, a vigil on the longest night. Choose the same answer two years running and it becomes a tradition. From then on it comes up first every year, keeping it pleases everyone, and breaking it disappoints them.

li.text:
The letter says when a choice is a tradition, and when choosing it again will make one. Keeping a tradition gives everyone a good memory; breaking one gives a bad one and resets the count. New, kept and broken traditions are written into the chronicle and the year's annals, and someone usually writes about a new tradition in their journal.
Traditions cost something every year, so only start the ones you can afford in a bad year too.
Days on the colony calendar grow into traditions the same way: keep one three years running (founding day, harvest day, a day you named) and the colony expects it. See "the colony calendar".

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: friends, rivals, comrades and mentors
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The bonds between colonists: how they form, grow, sour and end, and what they change.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Colonists who work side by side don't always end up friends.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists form lasting bonds out of how they feel about each other and what they go through. Steady liking turns into friendship, steady loathing into rivalry, fighting side by side into comradeship, and a skilled colonist may take an eager learner under their wing. Every bond has a strength and a short history, shown on the council's Bonds page.

li.heading: The four bonds

table.li: Bond | How it forms | How it ends
Friends | Two colonists' opinions of each other stay high enough. | It drifts with how they feel, and ends when it fades to nothing.
Rivals | Their opinions of each other stay low enough. | The same way as a friendship.
Comrades | Fighting in the same battle: drafted, manning a turret or attacking the enemy. Everyone who does becomes comrades. | It slowly fades between battles.
Mentor and student | A mentor (skill 12+, with a passion) teaches a student (skill 7 or less, with a passion) every day. | The student graduates at level 11, and both are proud.

li.after: Bonds add opinion, more at each stage: new, solid, deep. To keep a skill in the colony after your best worker dies, look for a mentorship on the Bonds page, or have a learner with a passion work alongside them.

li.heading: What moves a bond
li.text:
Small social events happen most days: late talks, pranks, snubs, squabbles, war stories, lessons, contests, gifts, gossip and the odd truce. Life brings its own: a friend keeping vigil at a sickbed, an evening at a camp on the map, a quarrel over what the council decided, fears confided in the night, grief carried together, homesickness shared, a peace offering after a quarrel. Each moves the bond a little. Keep rivals on different work shifts to avoid squabbles.
The council's decisions feed back too. Losing an election to someone, having your wish passed over for theirs, a fight, a grudge from a dilemma or arguing over a decree can start rivalries. Backing the same petition, making up or going through something together builds friendships.

li.heading: Moments and frictions
li.text:
Smaller still are the moments colonists share in conversation, picked among the game's own chats: grieving together, talking shop, a story by the fire, a friendly contest. Who they are shapes them: night owls keep each other company in the small hours, undergrounders praise the rock overhead, brawlers compare scars, an iron-willed colonist steadies a nervous one, two gourmands plan a feast. So does what is going on: someone visits a sick friend or swears by an old remedy, two who spoke at the council talk it over afterward, the colony watches a camp's fires from the wall, and with the heart on a frightened colonist confides in a friend or a grateful one says thanks again. Frictions are the other side: chores, snoring, a borrowed knife, an annoying voice, a pyromaniac near the tinder, a nudist at the supper table, someone keeping their distance from the sick, a spat about the camp, a temper running high. The home has its own nuisances, each read from the real map, so fixing the cause is the cure: a sticking door, a leaking roof, a cramped or smoky room, a generator by the bed, a filthy room, a cold or stifling one, an animal in the bed, building work next to it, vermin indoors, a bare earth floor.
Moments, frictions and social events tell one story between the same two people. After a spat nothing warm passes between them until it wears off (usually half a day to a day, half as long again with an abrasive or volatile one of them, a day and a half after a falling-out) or one of them makes up, and a spat right after a warm moment is unlikely. A peace offering only comes after a quarrel.

li.heading: Circles
li.text:
Three to six colonists held together by strong friendships form a circle, and a strong circle votes as a bloc. Colonists outside every circle, with no close friend, sometimes feel left out.
Let someone's wish lapse and their close friends trust the council a little less, and those in the same circle lose slightly more.

li.heading: What bonds change
li.text: Friends and circle members back each other's wishes and petitions and vote for each other; rivals object to each other's wishes and vote against each other. A colonist's bonds and circle are listed in their trust tooltip on the Wishes page. When a bonded colonist dies, the ones left behind write about it.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: dreams
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What colonists dream about, and the rare dream that changes something or comes true.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: What a colonist dreams about is usually what's been bothering them.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A colonist who sleeps (or lies unconscious) for four hours or more may wake from a dream. Dreams grow out of their life: the battle two days ago, the friend they lost, the rival who insulted them, the wish the council ignored, the leg they no longer have, the skill they're learning. Most dreams are just a passing mood and a line in their journal. Hover over the mood in their Needs tab to read the dream itself.

li.heading: What they dream about
li.text:
Dreams about what really happened (a raid, a death, an insult, a broken promise, an illness, an addiction) are far more likely than others. People in their lives turn up: friends, rivals, partners, family, comrades, teachers and students, bonded animals, and the dead they loved.
Unhappy colonists have more nightmares, and volatile ones more still. Recurring nightmares usually mean a colonist is unhappy; check their Mood tab for the cause.

li.heading: What they feel, and what's around them
li.text:
With the heart turned on, feelings bring dreams of their own, likelier the stronger the feeling. A colonist angry at someone argues with them all night (and the rivalry grows a little); one grateful to someone repays the debt in a dream (and likes them a little more); envy dreams of someone else's life. Fear, dread, shame, loneliness, homesickness, despair, pride, hope, curiosity, restlessness, contentment and joy each have their dreams too.
Ailments color dreams: a toothache brings dreams of loose teeth, a cold or a cough dreams of breathing underwater, insomnia dreams of lying awake, bites and rashes dreams of itching, a bad back or a kidney stone dreams of carrying a millstone, and getting over an illness dreams of being strong again. So does the world around them: a camp on the map, a council meeting they spoke at or missed, sickness, famine, fighting or a fair in the region (world events), and the time of year.

li.heading: Dreams that change something
li.text: Now and then a dream leaves more than a mood behind:

points.li: an inspiration
a lesson in a skill
a good night's rest
a nightmare that leaves them shaken
a dream of a won fight that steadies their aim
a softened rivalry
a wish

li.heading: Omens
li.text:
Rarely, a dream is an omen, and a few days later it comes true: a caravan, a newcomer, falling cargo pods, a cold snap, a raid. Only one omen waits at a time. When a colonist wakes up talking about torches in the dark, check your defenses.
You can turn omens off with "Dreams that come true" in the settings.

li.heading: Telling them
li.text: Colonists tell each other their dreams, and telling someone you dreamt about them makes them like you a little more. Recent dreams are listed on the Dreams page, and dreams that came true go in the chronicle and the year's annals.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: life goals
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What each colonist has set their heart on doing before they die.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A wish takes a few days to grant. A life goal can take years.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A few days after settling in, each colonist sets their heart on something: master a craft, marry for love, have a child, find three true friends, train a student, make peace with a rival, earn a seat on the council or a name the colony remembers, a bedroom fit for a noble, a warrior's or a builder's record, or simply to live three more years. Children have goals of their own (a best friend, a skill, growing up), the old may want a grandchild or one more year, believers a role in their faith, and some only want to feel at home. The Roster page shows everyone's goal and how close they are; the page "every life goal" lists them all.

li.heading: How a goal is chosen
li.text:
Goals fit the person: passions, traits and situation decide what they want. A psychopath doesn't dream of true friends; an ascetic doesn't want a noble's bedroom.
Life sets them too. A battle can make a warrior, a brush with death a healer or someone who just wants more years, a wedding someone who wants to marry, a birth someone who wants a child, a lost election someone who wants a seat, and loneliness someone who wants friends. Seeing a friend achieve their goal can make them want the same. Something big can change their mind about a goal they've barely started.

li.heading: Getting there
li.text:
Once they're three quarters of the way there, they get a small, steady mood lift. Achieving it brings a letter, a long good mood, a big jump in trust, often an inspiration, and gladness among their friends, and it goes into the chronicle and the year's annals. After a while they may choose another goal, never the same one twice.
Check the Roster page now and then. A colonist one level short of mastery is worth a few days at their workbench. Goals like marriage, friends or peace with a rival can't be ordered, but shared work, shared rooms and shared battles help them along. Some dreams are about a colonist's goal, and some dilemmas come up because of one.

li.heading: Goals left unfinished
li.text: A colonist who dies before reaching their goal is remembered for it: the chronicle notes what they never got to do, and their friends write about it. The person who loved them most may take the goal up and finish it for them.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: secrets, vendettas and eulogies
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What colonists hide, who they can't forgive, and how they say goodbye.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Not everyone talks about where they came from.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Some colonists carry a secret, often from the life their backstory hints at: a raider's past, noble blood, a deserter's shame, a child left behind, a borrowed name, a hidden kindness. You won't know what it is; the Bonds page only shows when they confide in a close friend.

li.heading: Confiding and coming out
li.text:
Confiding brings relief and brings them closer. A confidant who later becomes their rival is likely to let it slip; a close friend rarely does. Someone at rock bottom may blurt it out themselves. So watch who confides in whom: if those two fall out, the secret will probably come out.
When a secret comes out, everyone reacts according to their nature: the kind forgive, the hard despise, the greedy envy, the abrasive mock. Betraying a confidence makes enemies. Some secrets put the council on the spot with a dilemma.
A secret the colonist never told anyone dies with them. If they told someone, it comes out at the funeral.

li.heading: Vendettas
li.text:
When raiders kill or carry off someone, the people who loved them swear vengeance on that faction. They carry it as a weight, fight harder when that faction shows up again, and are avenged once three of the enemy fall to them.
Those who swore vengeance take peace with the killers as a betrayal. It may still be worth it, but think twice before making peace with a faction that killed someone well loved.

li.heading: Quirks
li.text: Colonists also pick up quirks from what they live through, at most two at a time:

points.li: a lucky helmet worn through a fight (good mood with it, bad without)
a dread of storms after a death
a battle ritual
night prayers after a dream came true
a fear of the dark after lying downed
grief that returns every winter
harmless habits like knocking on wood or talking to the dead
red is bad luck, after a bad fight (uneasy when wearing red)
checking the gate every night, after a fight
always cold, after a night spent freezing; watching the stars, after a night slept outside

li.after: Most fade after a season or two. They're listed in the trust tooltip.

li.heading: Habits
li.text: Other quirks simply grow out of who someone is, now and then: a grower who talks to the plants (glad while growing, plant work 3% faster), a handler who names every animal (glad while handling, taming and training 3% likelier), a cook who sings at the stove (glad while cooking, 15% fewer food poisonings), an early riser (glad in the morning, sorry when kept up late), someone who hums at work, collects pretty stones for their room, can't stand a mess (unhappy in a dirty room, cleans 10% faster), feeds the birds, remembers every birthday (social impact up 3%), is always whittling (bored more slowly), talks in their sleep or saves the best bite for last. A habit's knack lasts as long as the habit, which fades after most of a year.

li.heading: Coming of age
li.text: With children (Biotech), coming of age is marked: parents are proud, the colony remembers the child they were, and the council is asked to help choose a path, often an apprenticeship that starts a real mentorship with the colony's best.

li.heading: After a death
li.text:
Half a day or so after someone dies, the person closest to them speaks at the grave. What they say depends on who the dead were: their years here, the name they earned, the goal they never reached, who killed them.
A dead colonist's weapon or hat passes to the person who loved them most. Carrying it is a comfort (to anyone, more to the heir), and losing it hurts.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: strangers, beasts and pets
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Visitors, traders, prisoners, fallen enemies, nemeses, wild animals and the colony's own animals.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A raider who gets away may come back with the next raid.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists don't only deal with each other. While visitors, a trade caravan, guests or prisoners are around, and every day among the colony's animals and the wildlife, small moments happen: news from the road, haggling, words through a cell door, a fallen raider's plea, a pet's mischief, a stag at dawn. Some put a hard choice to the council. And an enemy who badly hurts one of yours and gets away becomes that colonist's nemesis.

li.heading: Visitors and prisoners
li.text:
Encounters happen a few times a day at most, and never during a fight. Visitors and traders make them likelier while they're here. Warm moments make visitors like the colonist (their opinion of them rises), sometimes improve goodwill with their people, and count toward the "known far and wide" life goal. Let your most sociable colonists host visitors: good impressions add up to goodwill, and sometimes to a new recruit.
With prisoners, kind words soften them (less resistance); taunts and cruelty sour moods on both sides.
Council choices about strangers come with short deadlines when the stranger is only passing through: a visitor who wants to stay, a trader who wants an heirloom, beggars at the gate, a wounded raider who's still breathing.

li.heading: Nemeses
li.text:
A nemesis is an enemy who struck down, maimed or killed a colonist and lived. A raider who flees is remembered, and may ride with the next raid from their people. A wild animal that mauls someone and slinks off gets a name and keeps prowling.
Capturing a nemesis, or seeing them dead, lifts the mood of the one they hurt. Doing it by their own hand lifts them most, and completes the "settle the score" life goal.

points.li: When a nemesis returns, put the one they hurt somewhere safe, or somewhere they can finish it themselves. Either way, expect a big swing in their mood.
Capture fallen raiders who downed your people: a nemesis in your cells can't come back with the next raid.
Hunt a named beast as a group. It already beat one of you.

li.heading: The colony's animals
li.text: An animal that fights beside its person in a battle is remembered for it. A named animal that dies gets a farewell from the one who loved it.

li.heading: The land, the seasons and the weather
li.text:
Some moments only happen in their place or their hour. In the desert a wild animal shares the noon shade; on the tundra and in the northern forest there are tracks in the snow and travelers with tricks against the cold; in jungle and swamp, eyes in the undergrowth, a cape of leaves in the rain, lights over the marsh at night; in the mountains, an animal on the ridge and news of the high passes; on the coast, the tide line and the sea in a storm. Spring brings the first green, fall the creatures getting ready for winter, and rain, fog, snow, thunder and a clear night each have moments of their own.
Rimfolk reads the land from the biome's name and the map tile (hills, mountains, a coast, a river), so the biomes other mods add count too: a mod's mangrove is a swamp. The everyday encounters have lines for each kind of land as well.

li.heading: Strangers from your other mods
li.text: Some moments only come with a mod that brings the stranger: Hospitality's guests talk about their room and their home and may ask to stay, visitors of the Empire or of Vanilla Expanded's republics and settlers talk about their own people, traveling mages and fighters of A RimWorld of Magic share a working or a form, and Alpha Animals' creatures are met by name. With Medieval Overhaul, visitors notice the colony's cheese, wine, hearth and books once it has them. The Almanac page "What Rimfolk does with your mods" lists what's in your game.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: the colony's character
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How the council's choices add up to a reputation: merciful or harsh, generous or thrifty, and more.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Turn away enough beggars and word gets around.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every answer to a dilemma, every decree and many granted wishes say something about who the colony is. Lean far enough one way and word spreads: the colony becomes known as merciful, thrifty, hard-working or guarded, and later renowned for it. Colonists are proud of ways that suit their nature and chafe at ways that don't. The "Our ways" page in the council window shows where the colony stands, who is proud, who chafes, and what shaped it.

li.heading: The five ways

table.li: Way | Who likes it
Merciful or harsh | Kind colonists like mercy; the bloodthirsty and psychopaths like harshness.
Generous or thrifty | Kind colonists like generosity; the greedy like thrift.
Traditional or restless | The old like tradition; the young like change.
Open or guarded | Sociable people like openness.
Hard-working or easygoing | The industrious like hard work; the lazy like ease.

li.after: Colonists whose nature fits the colony's ways get up to +4 mood; those whose nature clashes get up to -4. Decide what kind of colony you want to be, and let the council's answers follow: a colony that sticks to its ways keeps the colonists who share them happy. Check "Our ways" before recruiting, since a kind recruit will chafe in a harsh colony.

li.heading: Earning and losing a name
li.text:
Each way runs from -100 to 100. The colony is known for a way at 25 and renowned at 60, and loses the name a little below that. An answer given by default, when the council didn't decide in time, counts half.
Old deeds slowly fade, so a colony can change its name: about half of a way is forgotten in a year, and the further the colony already leans, the less each new deed adds. To change it on purpose, choose the other way for a while.

li.heading: With the neighbors
li.text:
A generous or open colony slowly gains goodwill with its neighbors as word gets around; a thrifty or guarded one slowly loses a little. Being open and generous is a slow, cheap way to keep neighbors friendly.
Some encounters and dilemmas only come up for a colony with a certain name: refugees seeking a merciful colony, traders who heard you count every grain.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: reading moods
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The Mood tab and the Moods page: what weighs on your colonists, why, and what to do about it.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Most bad moods come from something you can build: a table, a light, a bed.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every colonist has a Mood tab next to their Needs: each mood with its size, why it's there, when it fades, which mod it comes from, and what you can do about it. The council window's Moods page adds up every mood in the colony, so you can see what weighs on everyone at once, who feels it, and who is closest to breaking.

li.heading: The Mood tab
li.text:
The mood bar shows where a colonist is, where their mood is heading, and the lines below which minor, major and extreme breaks become possible.
A memory fades on its own, and the Mood tab says when. A lasting mood stays while its cause does, so removing the cause is the only fix. Each mood with a known fix has a "what to do" line, with buttons that lead to the advisor's matching warning, the council page that deals with it, or an Almanac page. Moods from other mods get general advice based on what kind of mood they are, and their mod's name.
"Where it comes from" splits the mood between the base game, Rimfolk and each of your other mods, so you can see which mod is pushing hardest. When a colonist has it good, a "Good times" line under it says how much Rimfolk's balance takes off their good moods right now: good moods that add up slowly, good memories that fade sooner, and comforts that high standards make count for less. Hover it for the rules.
Click a section's heading (the heart, what weighs on them, what lifts them) to fold it away; it stays folded until you quit. Above a tall inspect pane, as with RimHUD, the tab gets shorter and scrolls.

li.heading: The Moods page
li.text:
Start at the top of "Weighing on the colony": the biggest totals usually have the cheapest fixes, like a dining table, lights or a bedroom. Check "Closest to breaking" before a long job or a caravan, and give the shakiest colonists something good first.
A colonist sinking toward a break line needs help now: a fine meal, recreation, a party or rest, while you fix the cause.

li.heading: What colonists fix themselves
li.text: They tidy their room, visit a grave, take a break when worn down, or plan a cheap light, plant pot, passive cooler or sleeping spot for their own room. You get a message each time.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: Rimfolk events
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What comes to the colony from outside: pasts catching up, challenges, old enemies, the land and the sky, visitors with a purpose.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Sooner or later, someone from a colonist's old life comes looking for them.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every few days something comes to the colony from outside: an old comrade asks for a colonist by name, a traveling champion wants a contest, a comet hangs in the sky, mourners come to a grave. These are Rimfolk's own events. They join your storyteller's own random events and follow its rhythm, or, if you prefer, come on Rimfolk's own timer (a setting). The bigger happenings across the whole region are world events, with a page of their own. Many ask the council what to do; the answer shapes the colony's character, and often a colonist's life. Answer the letters: an unanswered one falls to a default, which is rarely the best choice.

li.heading: Pasts that catch up
li.text:
Who a colonist used to be (read from their backstory: soldier, outlaw, noble, trader, healer, scholar, farmer, artisan) decides which pasts can catch up with them. Bounty hunters only come for someone with a violent past. A colonist known by an epithet may be sought out by name.
A colonist who walked out or was banished may come back one day. A prisoner who dies in the colony's hands may be avenged by their people.

li.heading: Visitors
li.text:
Strangers who ask to join wait at the edge of the map until you answer. Use "Look at" in the letter to see who they are before you decide. Visitors, finds and inheritances fit the colony's era: a medieval colony meets medieval folk and digs up medieval things.
Contests with a traveling champion never hurt anyone: target shooting, wrestling without weapons, crafts, cooking, art, debate. The better one usually wins, and the letter says how good each side is, so read the odds before betting.
A traveling doctor's shots (or a herbalist's tonic) help everyone fight off sickness faster for a month. What a journalist or chronicler writes depends on the colony's character: mercy, generosity and openness make for a kind article, and their opposites for an unkind one.

li.heading: Hail, vermin and the great beast
li.text:
Hail only hurts crops out in the open. Vermin only get into food that isn't kept cold, and a cat or dog may catch them first. Roof a field or two and keep food cold, and most of the harm is gone.
The great beast is tougher than any of its kind. It leaves in a few days, and only fights if provoked. If you hunt it, hunt with a group, not a lone colonist.

li.heading: Orders, debts and waiting
li.text:
A neighbor's order is collected five days after you take it. Only goods in your stockpiles and shelves count, and it's the whole amount or nothing. Some answers take days to come back, like a caravan to a far market, a cart sent to a harvest fair, a relative on the way or a guest who wrote ahead.
The council window's World page shows each of these and when it's due, along with fights on their way, questions waiting for an answer, and who's out there with the colony on their mind.
Keep some silver in the stores. Debts, bounties, tribute and treasure maps all ask for it.

li.heading: Fights
li.text: Fights only come if the settings allow Rimfolk events that can end in a fight, only when the storyteller sends threats at all, never on top of another fight, and at a share of the storyteller's own raid strength. Everyday events (stranded merchants, a tinker, a neighbors' quarrel, an old grave, a family visit, a fortune teller and others) never end in a fight. A band of the people someone swore vengeance on can be drawn into a fight at home, if you want it.

li.heading: Events that remember
li.text: Some events follow from earlier ones: a deserter's old unit, a lost child come back grown, a rematch with a champion, the great beast's young, grateful pilgrims. A neighbor whose order you filled may come back to buy again, the runaway lovers' family may come asking after them, a relative who visited may write (and can be invited to stay), and neighbors remember how you judged their quarrel. The colony's founding day comes once a year.

li.heading: The land, the season and the era
li.text: Some events only come where and when they fit: a flush of mushrooms after rain in a mild, wet place, white nights near the poles in summer, a desert in bloom after rare rain, the long rains where it's hot and wet, an ice fair on a frozen river, the first snow, the longest night of winter, an eclipse. Callers fit the colony's era: a tribal colony may get a spirit singer, a medieval one a scribe, an industrial or spacer one a photographer or a tourist.

li.heading: Callers who touch the colony's life
li.text:
Some callers only come when there's something for them to do. A bonesetter comes while someone is nursing an everyday ailment, and can ease it or cure it. A fiddler comes while someone is strained, and an evening of music takes some of the strain off. Guests who want to watch a council meeting come only once meetings are on. A peacemaker comes for two colonists who can't stand each other. A camp nearby can bring a shared feast, or a quarrel to settle.
Many answers call on someone with the right skill or trait: a good cook, a healer, a builder, a crafter who can teach. The letter names who it would be once you choose; when nobody at home fits, the answer is greyed out and says why.

li.heading: Stories in stages
li.text: A few events are the first stage of a longer story told over days or weeks: a door in the hill, a fugitive at night, a feud in a nearby town, a preacher on the road, a lost expedition, a bundle of lost letters, a stranger's seeds, a play written about the colony. The colony's answer, and luck settled when it matters, decide which stage comes next and when. The World page shows what's coming, and each story ends in one of several ways, written into the chronicle.

li.heading: Missions
li.text: Now and then a neighbor asks for something done by a deadline: tame a runaway prize animal, raise a shrine for pilgrims, supply a funeral or a wedding, help a town rebuild after a fire, a storm or a flood (wood, stone blocks or more wood, cloth, and steel or components for an industrial town), or send provisions for a hard winter, a dry year or a sickhouse (raw food or pemmican, meals, medicine, cloth, firewood). Only goods in your stockpiles count. All of it pays well over its worth; at least half pays its plain worth; less, and they go elsewhere and think less of the colony.

li.heading: With other mods
li.text: A few events only come with certain mods.

table.li: Mod | Event
A RimWorld of Magic | Lights falling from the sky
Alpha Animals | A strange creature
Dubs Bad Hygiene | Travelers asking for a bath
Hospitality | A guest of note who judges your guest room

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: scenarios with stakes
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Rimfolk's scenarios start the game with something already in motion: a friend on the way, a mentorship, an enemy, a debt, a feud, a prisoner.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Not every colony starts with a clean slate.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Rimfolk adds ten scenarios, marked "(Rimfolk)" on the scenario page along with how hard they are. Four are small, gentle starts with one or two colonists and no attacks of their own (The Inheritance, Master and Apprentice, Runaway Hearts, The Lone Hunter); six come with stakes (Hot Money, Marooned, Deserters, Bad Blood, Borrowed Time, The Fallen Tyrant). A few seconds into the game a letter says how things stand. Their pieces are scenario parts you can add to any scenario in the editor.

table.li: Scenario | What to know
Hot Money | Decide early whether you're keeping the silver. Spending it and then refusing to pay it back is the worst of both.
Marooned | Someone in the pods is lying. Keep the friendships strong and the truth will come out sooner.
Bad Blood | Friendships across the two families matter most. Shared work, shared meals and a common enemy all help.
Borrowed Time | Trade from day one. Half the debt paid on time buys three weeks.
The Fallen Tyrant | The tyrant is out cold for the first few hours. Build a cell with a bed before the drug wears off.

li.heading: Sworn enemies and hunts
li.text:
A sworn enemy is a nemesis from the first day. If their people hunt the colony, they come a set number of times, a month or so apart. The hunt ends sooner if that enemy dies, joins the colony or is sold off, or if their people make peace or are wiped out.
The "Fights in Rimfolk's scenarios" setting makes those attacks weaker or stronger, and your storyteller's difficulty scales them too. Fights a scenario promises come even with Rimfolk events that can end in a fight switched off, but only when the storyteller sends threats at all.

li.heading: Debts
li.text: A debt comes due as a letter with three answers:

points.li: Pay it.
Pay half and ask for more time. The rest grows by about a third, and they only wait twice.
Refuse, and meet the collectors.

li.after: Unanswered, a debt counts as refused. Debts and hunts are on the World page.

li.heading: Feuds and arrivals
li.text:
Two feuding families each take one surname. Family members like each other more, and dislike the other family; the grudge fades over a couple of months if nothing feeds it.
Someone from the past, a visiting scholar or a great beast arriving "around a set day" waits for a quiet moment. If they can't come yet (the wrong season, nobody fits), they try again the next day.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: feelings and strain
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Strain wears colonists down over days; feelings color their wishes, dreams and moments; four needs show what their life is missing.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A high mood doesn't mean someone is fine. Check their strain after a hard week.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
Mood says how a colonist feels today. Strain, from 0 to 100, says how worn down they are: it builds slowly from fighting, pain, losses and bad nights, and comfort can't buy it off quickly. Alongside it, each colonist has one or two feelings at a time (grief, fear, pride, joy and others) and four long-term needs of the heart.
None of this changes how the game decides on mental breaks. Vanilla mood stays the number that counts. Strain reaches the game only through one mood of its own, a small slowdown at work, darker dreams and, at the very end of the rope, a day off; feelings and needs never add mood at all.

li.heading: What builds strain

table.li: Source | How much
Fighting | 4 an hour while drafted or attacked with enemies on the map (12 a day at most)
Pain and serious injuries | up to 6 a day
Being downed | 3 an hour (8 a day at most)
Deaths and losses | 4 for a colonist's death, 5 for seeing an ally die, 8 for family, each memory once (14 a day at most)
Long days without sleep, no free time | up to 4 and 3 a day
Bad nights (cold, heat, noise, outside, on the ground) | 1 or 2 for each, once a night (4 a day at most)
A dark home (under a roof, not the night sky), hunger, very low mood | up to 2, 4 and 6 a day
Hard council decisions | decrees they resent (1 to 3 a day) and dilemma outcomes that hurt (4 a day at most)
Fear, grief, worry and despair | up to 2 or 3 a day while they last

li.after: Everything together adds at most about 25 a day. Iron-willed colonists take 40% less and steadfast ones 20% less; nervous ones take 25% more and volatile ones 40% more. Psychopaths take nothing from deaths, the bloodthirsty little from fighting, masochists nothing from pain. The strength setting makes all of it build from 50% to 150% as fast.

li.heading: What drains it
li.text:
Strain drains by itself in quiet hours (0.15 an hour), faster asleep in a bed at a comfortable temperature (0.6 an hour, 0.25 elsewhere) and during recreation (0.5 an hour). A good mood speeds this up by a quarter, a very good one by half. Joy, pride, hope and calm speed it further; despair and dread slow it. When all four needs of the heart are at 60 or more, it drains 20% faster.
Some things take a chunk off at once: a party (6), a concert or a wedding (5), a festival, feast or celebration (3 to 8, 12 a day at most), a deep talk or a good moment with a friend (1.5 to 3, 6 a day at most), and a good cry (catharsis, 30). A colonist with a warm bed, free time and a decent mood sheds about 10 a day, so one hard day takes two or three to undo.

table.li: Strain | Band | What it does
0 to 29 | Steady | Nothing
30 to 54 | Strained | -3 mood, darker dreams
55 to 74 | Worn down | -5 mood, 5% slower work, more nightmares
75 to 100 | Near breaking | -8 mood, 10% slower work, many nightmares; from 85, a day off may come

li.heading: A day off
li.text:
At strain 85 or more, a colonist may simply stop: they keep to their room for six to twelve hours, eating and sleeping as they need, and do no work. A letter says why and what would help. It never happens in danger, while drafted or asleep, while hurt or sick, in the middle of caring for or carrying someone or fighting a fire, to children, slaves, prisoners or guests, or when fewer than two others could keep working; at most once in 2 days in the colony and once in 10 days for each colonist. It ends early if a threat appears, if they need a doctor, or if their room gets too cold or too hot. Afterwards their strain drops by about 40 (20 if it was cut short) and they feel lighter for a day and a half (+6 mood).
To head it off, use days of rest: a decree that slows everyone's work by 10% for three days and makes strain drain about twice as fast. Colonists may ask for it when the colony is worn down.

li.heading: Feelings
li.text: Feelings come from the moods a colonist has right now (as big as the game counts them) and from what they can see: enemies on the map, a fight on its way, a new face, quiet days. The strongest one or two show in the inspector; the Mood tab lists every one they have, how strong, since when and why. They add no mood, because that would count the same thing twice. Instead they nudge: a wish that fits becomes up to half again as likely, moments between colonists go warmer or pricklier, dreams change color, strain builds or drains faster. Each nudge is at its fullest only when the feeling is strong.

table.li: Feeling | Comes from | Nudges
Grief | deaths and losses | a grave for the dead, grief shared, dreams of the dead, some strain
Fear | danger here and now | defenses and weapons, nightmares, strain
Dread | what's coming: a promised fight, a warband, a lean winter | stores, medicine and defenses, a trickle of strain
Anger | insults, fights, unfair decisions, a rival | frictions, wishes for justice
Shame | a prisoner executed or sold, a break they regret | fewer warm moments, wishes that make amends
Envy | someone else's room or things, the council's favorite | frictions with them, the same things
Disgust | raw food, corpses, rot, filth | a clean colony, better food
Loneliness | no friends here, a partner away, left out | warm moments, a party, a companion
Homesickness | new here, family elsewhere | good food, keepsakes, dreams of home
Frustration | refusals, lapsed wishes, work they love turned off | less patience, frictions
Despair | long low spirits, loss after loss, a colony losing | slower recovery, a day off likelier
Joy | good meals, parties, wishes granted | faster recovery, warm moments, sweet dreams
Pride | good work, victories, a seat, a name | faster recovery, art and fine things
Love | a partner or children close by | warm moments, sweet dreams, less loneliness
Gratitude | rescued, tended, helped, a wish granted | warm moments with the one who helped, trust in the council
Hope | spring, a newcomer, healing, strain lifting | faster recovery, less despair
Awe | auroras, eclipses, the comet, beautiful things | art, flowers, a shrine, very rarely an inspiration
Contentment | quiet days with needs met | faster recovery
Curiosity | research, books, visitors, new land | books, lessons, journeys
Restlessness | the same work every day, too little fun | time outside, travel, a hunt

li.heading: The heart's needs

table.li: Need | Met by | Makes likelier
Belonging | friends here, a partner, family, a circle, good moments | parties, companions, a wedding; goals about friends and family
Purpose | work they love, a life goal, a seat, learning | a space for their craft, lessons; goals of mastery
Safety | no danger, food, medicine, defenses, their health | defenses, armor, an infirmary; goals of a fighter
Freedom | time outdoors, free time, varied work, travel, few restrictions | time outside, travel, a hunt; goals of discovery

li.after: Each runs from 0 to 100 and is worked out every hour; none gives mood. The one a colonist lacks most (below 45) makes what answers it up to 35% likelier, and when all four are at 60 or more, strain drains 20% faster.

li.heading: Where to see it
li.text:
The Mood tab has a Heart section: the strain meter with its band, what built it lately, what would help, every feeling and the four needs. The council's Moods page lists who is worn down. A short line in the inspector reads like "Strain: worn down · restless, proud", and RimHUD can show strain, feelings and needs. Hover the strain mood in the Needs tab to see what built it up.
Settings, on the Heart & health page: feelings and strain on or off, the day off, the inspector line, and how quickly strain builds.
